utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Dzolic, good morning to you as well. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that that solemn declaration still binds you. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First matter I would like to raise with you, Mr. Dzolic, is so that you can look at the diagram showing the structure of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we put on the screen, please, 2D06-0009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dzolic, this document will set out in a diagram form some of the details that you were telling us about in your evidence yesterday and gave in your statement. And at the top of this diagram, can you see the military police administration of the Ministry of Defence, where the chief of administration is General Lausic? Is that right that he's in charge of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he has a deputy chief of administration, and that's Brigadier Biskic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And their headquarters are in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then, also, on this diagram, you will see a red arrow down and then a number of battalions listed: The 66th, with a commander in Zagreb; the 67th; the 68th; the 71st; 73rd; 72nd; 69th; 70th; and 74th. Is that right to say that those battalions and companies are all subordinated to General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection and to the best of my knowledge, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see in the box where there is the 72nd, we see the commander of the 72nd, Colonel Budimir. Is that right that he was the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he had a deputy, Major Primorac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were a member of the 72nd. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also subordinated to General Lausic, we also see on this diagram, first of all, a traffic company. Is it right that there was a separate division in relation to traffic for the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was one at the level of the administration in that period, but it is possible. I don't discount that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There's an anti-terrorist platoon of the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it in this diagram, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the 7th Light Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a military police training centre in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just get a clarification as to what the -- who has prepared this diagram and what the source is. I know there is a reference to sources at the bottom, but it looks to me from the face of the document to be a document prepared by the Defence team, and if that could be mentioned on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how it look, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Rather than bringing piles of books in the courtroom, we've chosen to do it in a simple way, declaring on the document where the sources are from for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that satisfy?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, may I make this document an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D785 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just while we're looking at this document, I'd just like to ask you a few questions about training, Mr. Dzolic. What sort of training you had before you became a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of training you had to become a military policeman? Did you go on a course; if so, how long was the course? What sort of training did you have?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: The -- my training and preparation in the training centre is something that was never carried out; however, my authority to act stemmed from my work as a military policeman over a period of five years in military police units. I cannot recall with any certainty when the military police training centre was established, as of what date, and when members or employees of the military police began to be sent to the training centre from the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I wish to mention that before the outbreak of the homeland war, I used to be a judicial policeman, where, as a judicial policeman, for nine months I was trained in Zagreb, in order to be granted the powers of a judicial policeman. I hope that this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Dzolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just mention, and I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Kay. Just the sources that are on this chart really do not indicate a date or any specific cities with which we could check so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that rather than interrupting Mr. Kay at this moment, if you need further details, that he will be willing to provide them to you so that you can check. I don't know whether that has to be done during the cross-examination or whether -- Mr. Kay, are you willing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is all very basic information that comes from the Prosecution's own files and sources of information, and that's what we have used to compile this. This is very basic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, reference is made to decisions and orders, and it could well be that there is only one order by that name. But could you assist Ms. Mahindaratne on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will gladly get one of my team to put a bundle together for her, so that she can see what the law is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Mr. Dzolic, the information given to me was you may have said you never conducted training rather than not being trained. The question was the training that you had, whether you personally had any training within the military police.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, when I was an ordinary military policeman, just a private, there were neither the means nor was there the time for any kind of training in that respect. Training, if one can call it that, was conducted through the practical implementation of tasks on the ground. I did go through that sort of training in my everyday assignments. But for someone to train me and educate me strictly for the tasks of a military policeman, that's something that never happened in the training centre, not as regards the work of a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at another document, again in diagrammatic form. Could the Registry produce 2D06-0011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, will we at a later stage receive further understanding of what the arrows exactly mean going in one direction or in two directions or what the boxes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I want to not delay this witness too long perhaps on fine detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This, again, is another diagram reflecting what you've put in your statement, what you've told us about in evidence, and with a few extra details, so that there is an complete picture of the structure of the 72nd Battalion. Can you see that, Mr. Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we look at the top of the boxes there, we see the 72nd Battalion. The commander was Colonel Budimir. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Deputy Commander was Major Primorac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And subordinated to him were companies of the 72nd Battalion, and can you see there the companies: The 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also the traffic company, which had a lieutenant in charge of it. Was that also one of the companies of the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also formed was the independent company that was based in Knin, and that was called the 7th Company. And we know that you were appointed on the 5th of August as the commander of that, having been originally in the joined company in Rujani. And you were the commander of that from the 29th of July to the 5th of August, and then the independent company became the 7th Company. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is correct. But, as far as I can remember, while I was the commander of that company, it was not the 7th Company. It was only about ten days after I left Knin that it -- when it was given that name. It was a joint company. That's what we used to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The dotted arrows there reflect that the members of your company were drawn from the other companies of the 72nd, so that to form the joined company, various police officers from the other companies were sent to join you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I just ask Mr. Kay if there is an English version of this chart available that we could follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find it on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- my computer on the English channel, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now it's on my screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And all those companies were subordinated to Colonel Budimir. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what the diagram shows, and that's how it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And other than the companies, there were also other sections and squads which made up the 72nd, and you told us yesterday about the criminal section of the military police, which is also subordinated to Colonel Budimir. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a logistics platoon, and an anti-terrorist platoon, and a dog section. Were those also other squads, sections, platoons subordinated to Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it right, as reflected in this diagram, that you didn't have a criminal section within your company, the joint company, which was based in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that question, Mr. President. That evidence is already in. In fact, the witness clearly answered this question yesterday, and if -- I could tell Court what the witness said if the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Court, of course, can read what the witness said. First of all, of course, the Chamber will consider whether questions are repetitious, and, of course, we're not seeking repetition. I don't know, Mr. Kay, if this may be an introduction to further questions. So if I would stop every question that would be put for the second time, we might lose time by me stopping counsel. We might gain a lot of time by avoiding repetitious questions. However, I have another problem with the question, in light of the evidence given yesterday by the witness. This reflects -- the diagram reflects part only - I'm not saying that this does not reflect what he said yesterday - but it certainly does not reflect everything he said yesterday on criminal sections. So, to that extent, the reference to what the chart shows, the chart shows part of his evidence and exactly the part you refer to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that right what I've put to you, that the independent company in Knin did not a criminal section within that company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's not right. As of the 8th of August -- actually, this was the 8th -- or, rather, this was the joint company. It had not been formed according to the establishment. It was created as a joint company and it was dislocated from the battalion headquarters, so that as of the 8th of May [as interpreted], employees of the criminal police were added to the Knin company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 8th of May of what year?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: 1995, on our entry into the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the witness is confusing the 5th day of the eighth month with the 8th day of the fifth month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm told he said, "August," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you have a criminal section that was part of the independent company in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As of the 8th of August, 1995, three or four policemen were attached to my company. I can't confirm the exact number who arrived on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: They were subordinated to me in the sense that they were supposed to carry out their everyday tasks in the company; for example, lining up at lunch-time, their appearance, their conduct had to be the same as that of every other member of the company. However, in their professional work, they were subordinated to the military crime police department, which we see in the diagram here, and this was under the leadership of Corporal Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that explains that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this document be admitted into evidence as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D786 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us turn now to the evidence that you gave yesterday concerning the establishment of the 72nd. You were shown various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have D267 first, and page 4 of six in the English version where we will be looking at paragraph 10. This is the document dated the 2nd of August. It is from the military police administration to all the military police battalions, and it was issued by General Lausic on that day. And it is in this document that Major Juric is appointed and a group of officers from the regular military police section of the -- and the military police administration crime section to assist in commanding and organizing the activities of the 72nd and 73rd Battalion that shall perform tasks in its own area of responsibility and provide necessary assistance to the 72nd. Those commanders of the 72nd and 73rd shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, Major Juric, was he from the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a major, he was in command of the 72nd and 73rd Battalions; but as we've looked, the 72nd Battalion had a colonel in command, and that was Colonel Budimir. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's right. However, as far as I can remember, I don't know whether Colonel Budimir was a colonel at that time or a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll look at a document in a moment which will tell us what his rank was. But if he was a colonel and a major was appointed as his superior, would that be an appointment and command that you would have to accept as being from a superior officer, although he was a major?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's say Colonel Budimir -- let's say Budimir was a colonel and there's evidence that he was a colonel. Major Juric, as a major, although that is an inferior rank to a Colonel. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because of the order that had made him the commander and superior to the other commanders, the colonels of the 72nd and 73rd, that would be an appointment and subordination that would you have to accept. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. I don't know what the foundation for that question is whether this witness is aware of exactly at that level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, he was member of that battalion. If the witness knows, he can answer it. The question is whether the appointment of a major in a position in the hierarchy higher than a colonel, whether that would result in a situation where the higher ranking but inferior-positioned colonel had to accept the orders of the major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear now, Your Honour. If this is an order regarding this, an officer may issue orders to a superior officer according to rank. It is the duty, as far as I can recall, always attached to it more power and authority than rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we just go to the next page, page 5, we see details of what reporting would take place for the 72nd and 73rd by Major Juric to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about now is some questions concerning Major Juric. Did you report to him while he was in command of the 72nd and 73rd?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that. There is no evidence that Major Juric was in command of the 72 and 73rd. The document says that the commanders are subordinated. There is no indication of the -- of Major Juric being -- I object to this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne. You are objecting against substance of the question; whereas, of course, in cross-examination, you are more free than you would be in examination-in-chief. And if you see that disasters are about to happen, I would not prevent you from intervening, but let's wait for the answer of the witness, to whom he reported. And if there's any issue as reporting to someone who apparently was not in command, because that seems to be the substance of your objection, then, of course, the next question arises why one would report to someone who was not in command then, of course, you can raise that issue during re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understood, it is my learned friend's own case, the Prosecution's own case, that Major Juric was in command of the 72nd in Knin at this period, and I do wonder what is happening here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is that something you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We do not confirm that Major Juric was in command. There was a different terminology used. We have not stated that Major Juric was in command of the 72nd military police. That is not -- that was my objection, in fact, the terminology used that he was in command. There was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not raise the issue again. You can do that in re-examination. There's no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, Mr. Kay, I would have to check exactly whether with all the details of the wording that's the Prosecution case or not. But if you have a clear source for that, I take it that you'll remind Ms. Mahindaratne of such a position; and if there's not, then, of course, there seems, at least in that respect, there seems to be no major problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, was Major Juric in command of the 72nd and the 73rd Military Police Battalions as of the 2nd of August, according to the orders of Major-General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: From what I can recall from that time, and also looking at this item here, where it says that the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd shall be subordinated to Major Juric, I can infer that he was a commander and that he was authorised to issue commands to those commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And may I remind the Court of the evidence of the witness Hill whom the Prosecution called on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Major Juric was someone that you knew at the time because you shared a room with him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did he command you whilst he was in Knin until you left?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at D268. This is a document dated the 2nd of August, 1995. It is a document, again, from General Lausic about the reinforcement of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and we see in his order his task is set out. In the command system, he is superior to the 2nd -- 72nd Military Police Battalion and 73rd Military Police Battalion commanders, with regard to the 73rd extending assistance to the 72nd. If we look at page 3 of the English, he is responsible for the implementation of all military police tasks in the 72nd military police zone of responsibility. He shall cooperate and coordinate the implementation of tasks of with the workers of the Zadar police administration. Other parties are named. He is authorised to undertake all measures to ensure efficient and effective implementation of military police tasks in the 72nd Military Police Battalion and operating group north -- Operation Group North zones of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was General Lausic's order in relation to Major Juric, and can you confirm that he did take command and was responsible for the implementation of all the military police tasks whilst you were there in Knin with the joint company?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that question because, again, the witness has testified on this yesterday. I specifically asked the -- the witness on this particular issues, and the witness has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the evidence the witness gave yesterday can be tested in cross-examination, Ms. Mahindaratne; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But to have the witness answer the same question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you confirm - and I do apologise, Mr. Dzolic, for this - but can you confirm that he was and did take command and implement all the tasks within the zone of responsibility of the 72nd whilst you were there in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can confirm that he was a commander of the military police forces while I was in Knin; in other words, in the combat area zones where the armed forces were engaged in combat. However, whether he actually carried out all the tasks that are ordered in this document, I cannot confirm that because I wasn't present with Major Juric at all the meetings and coordinating meetings mentioned here. I know that he went and attended certain meetings, both with the police and with the superior commands; however, I don't know -- or, rather, I don't remember exactly with whom these meetings were, when, and how many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just would like to note that there may be an issue in line 17 -- I'm sorry, in line 14 on page 17, regarding the interpretation, and if we could have that checked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, with the interpretation, we always have two matters; the first is whether this leads to misunderstanding or whether it is a detail for which we need our interpreters to check the accuracy of the translation at the end. Since you refer to it now, perhaps, Mr. Kay, you put the question again, which appears in line 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will talk to Mr. Kay to explain to him what the issue is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps if you could rephrase --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I know it. I have other language speakers who have been able to advise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they confirm that there may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you reformulate the question and get an answer which is not suffering from any imposition. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree he was the commander of the military police in the zones of responsibility of the 72nd and 73rd at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hope that clears up the issue for my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was a zone of responsibility ever identified to you for the joint company in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, while I was commander of that company, I was not aware of the area of responsibility of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that something that should have been explained to you or ordered to you as to the geographical area of responsibility for which you were the commander of the company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: When I was issued an order from Rujani to enter Knin, I was told to enter Knin and establish a company there; in other words, to provide all the necessities for their normal life and work, to secure the vital facilities, to set up check-points. And according to me, in my opinion, in my view, I should have been issued more specific tasks as to what geographical areas I was to cover around Knin town, which was a rather large area. I couldn't tell you exactly what the area was. But it was -- and the borders of that area with other companies, so that each company would exactly know what their jurisdiction was and what responsibilities they had for which areas, so that there wouldn't be any overlapping in the assignments. Throughout the time when I was in Knin, I never received such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've seen that you were given a number of men under your command from the other companies of the 72nd reinforced by men from the 73rd. Can you remember how many men in all you had under your command in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: The manpower, as far as I can recall, and I think I already said this in my statement, the men that entered with me in Knin were about 75 military policemen strong. However, on the next day, we received reinforcement, additional forces arrived from the seat of the -- the headquarters of the battalion, a reinforcement of some 80 military policemen; and while I was there, while I was the commander of the joint company in Knin, in those five or six days, there were about 140 military policemen under me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know the men under you? Had you worked with them before?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: With some I had; with some I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had previously been in the 2nd Company, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And some of the men from the 2nd Company formed part of the joint company. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first men that you had in Knin, about the 75, what -- how many of them did you know, what proportion? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot say it now with certainty, after all the time that has elapsed; but I don't think I would be very wrong if I said about 50 per cent of them. However, I would like to stress that the forces that entered Knin together with me, there were also members of the -- of the 66th Battalion of the military police that came from Rujani. In other words, part of the forces from Grahovo were pulled out and they came into Knin with me. So it wasn't just members of the 72nd within this joint company, there were also members of the 66th; and of those, some 20 or so military police, I knew no one. I met and got to know some of them in the field, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what sort of ranks were they that also formed this joint company? Did you -- what type of rank of soldier did you have beneath you in the company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think there was a captain and then a senior lieutenant, or a lieutenant. How many non-commissioned officers there were, I really can't recall. The rest were probably privates. Some of them may have privates of first class or second class. But which rank they held, I can't really say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you organise them into platoons or units? How did you achieve that.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: How did I organise this? I can't really recall what the criterion was to assign them; however, I assume that I was guided by the idea that members who were attached and who had been members of the 66th who were with me when we entered Knin and who had their own commander of, let's say, a squad commander, he would be responsible for those members. I also tried to organise the members of other companies in such a manner that if there was an officer from that company, that that officer remained their superior and that he be my subordinate within the company itself. I think this was the general method of work; however, in view of how much time has elapsed, I really cannot recall this with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it difficult with the soldiers whom you didn't know of 50 per cent of the first 75 to know what their competence was, what their training was, what tasks they could do, if you didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I didn't have the time to check their professionalism or their knowledge before we set off and when we entered Knin; however, the test was actually done after we entered Knin, when I inspected check-points and supervised the patrols and their work. In conversation with those police officers, I could draw certain conclusions as to what type of soldier they were. However, what I would like to say, Your Honour, is that during the difficult times of war, a commander doesn't really have a lot of time to assess and reassess individual men; rather, we had to delegate and assign them tasks, and then, in the course of their execution of the task, you could determine what kind of soldier they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you discover that some were good and some were bad at their jobs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't recall with certainty now. I don't remember that there were soldiers who made serious omissions in their work; however, I allow the possibility that some individuals may have carried out certain tasks better or worse than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of the extra troops that were sent to you as reinforcement, did you -- did you know any of those troops?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I got to know them when they came to assist me in the Operations Group North in the Rujani command, and they were dislocated to the area of the town of Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what ranks did you have amongst those extra troops that were sent to you? What was the makeup, the composition in terms of ranks of the units?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there was one captain, Sigura. The other commanders, I'm not sure whether there were any officers among them; and how many non-commissioned officers there were among them, I cannot confirm that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: There was certainly one captain; and the other commanders, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, learning about the competence of the troops whilst you're done there in Knin, was that difficult for you? Did it make it harder for you in the performance of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Well, certainly. That was one thing that made my work more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we look at another document now, 65 ter 1629. It's a document dated the 5th of August, 1995, and it's a report by Major Juric on the execution of tasks on the 5th of August, 1995. And in the English version, we can see on the first page that it refers to various units. On page 2 of the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document was admitted yesterday as P879.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see at 1.4, can you see, your name is mentioned as being in Knin with your company that you've told us about. And it states about your supervisory and control post at the town entry and exit, securing facilities of special importance, receiving prisoners of war, preventing violations of public law and order. This was the 5th of August. We can see at the end of this document that Major Juric signs this - we've no need to pull this up - and sends it to the military police administration. He's reporting as to the work of your company on that day. As it was on the 5th of August, I presume, would I be right in saying that you didn't have time to make a written report to him of all your tasks that you had done?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, after so much time has elapsed, I don't think I drew up a written report. I think I informed him orally and gave him all the points he needed to compile this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were reporting to him so that he could make the report as you were subordinate to him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After the 5th of August until you left Knin, did you have occasions when you gave written reports to Major Juric, telling him what your company had done during the day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any certainty that I did, but I think that most likely there would have been such written reports that I sent to Major Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. And did you know that he was sending your reports and information that you gave him to the military police administration in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with any certainty that I knew that, but I did assume that these were the points he would use to brief his superior command. It was the input.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how often during a day did you meet with Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it would all depend on the current situation. It differed from day to day. Depending on the needs, we would meet at least once a day, but sometimes as many as five or six times. However, Your Honours, I can't state with certainty that it was five times or six times or only once. It would all depend on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying that you didn't have a regular daily meeting with him that was at a fixed time each day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But he knew what you were doing as part of your tasks and he let you get on with your job. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when we looked at that previous report of his, about the check-point, is that something that you did of your own initiative when you arrived in Knin, set one up without anyone having to tell you to set one up?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I set up check-points on the first day, not on my own initiative, but based on an order from Colonel Budimir, who ordered me to carry out this task, before I left Rujani to go to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did Colonel Budimir give you any other instructions other than that when you left Rujani to go to Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He just gave me general tasks to set up the life and work of the company, to find a facility to quarter my company in, to set up barrier check-points. And it was up to me to assess the situation on the ground and decide where it would be most useful to set up check-points, to control exit and entry into and from the town, and to provide security for protected facilities. And what facilities these were exactly, that's something I was not told right away. So, to the best of my recollection, on the first day, on my entry into Knin, we did not secure a large number of facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Knin? Had you been there before?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Knin. Before the war, I may have passed through it on my way to Zagreb in a car once or twice. You drive down the street, but you can't really see how big the town is or how far it extends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was all information that you had to find out in the following days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About what facilities there were in Knin, what buildings there were in Knin, the layout of the town, that was all information that you had to learn after you arrived in Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Major -- when did you meet Major Juric after you entered Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall. I can't say with certainty whether it was the first night, the 5th of August, after my arrival in Knin, or whether it was on the following day; but I do allow for the possibility that it was the first night rather than the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did know from talking to him whether he was familiar with Knin, whether he knew about the town?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall a conversation of that kind, nor I do recall that I was able to gain an insight into the extent of his knowledge of the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Colonel Budimir come to Knin at any stage?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't assert that; but I think that on the first day, or, rather, the first evening, he was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with him while you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with Colonel Budimir whilst you were in Knin? Did he and you have meetings about your work, discuss your work whilst you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember any such meetings, except for the meeting we spoke about yesterday, I think, when I testified that I had been present at a meeting held on the 12th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you report to Colonel Budimir during this period whilst you were in Knin as to what you were doing, what was happening, and what the work of the joint company was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Reporting to Colonel Budimir about the incidents that were occurring and the tasks of the company in Knin was something I did through reporting in the course of my work whenever he came to Knin; and, as I recall, reports were sent from the company to the battalion concerning the implementation of the Knin company, of the work of the Knin company, for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the Knin company sent daily reports to Colonel Budimir. Was that in written form, written reports?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall now what kind of reports these were, but I think they should have been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That would have been the standard procedure. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was Colonel Budimir based in Knin or did he remain based in Rujani?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: The first night, after the company entered Knin, I can't be sure whether he was actually in Knin or whether he was carrying out some other tasks or whether he had gone back to the headquarters of the 72nd Battalion. I think it most likely that he was not in Rujani because, at that time, only a squad of military policemen remained in Rujani, and they were carrying out the tasks of securing the forward command post. Allow me to correct myself as regards my certainty. He may have been in Rujani if the commander of the Military District was holding a meeting in Rujani that evening, and it was necessary for Colonel Budimir to attend that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Colonel Budimir visit Knin every day after the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty that it was every day; but if it wasn't every day, it would be 90 per cent of the days while I was there, while I was the company commander in Knin, that I would meet with Colonel Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did he discuss your tasks and work?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall, probably yes, but you'd have to ask Colonel Budimir that, because I don't remember whether he discussed my work or not. I don't, however, recall any objections to or any criticism of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He remained your immediate superior, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did he supervise your work, tell you what tasks to do?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As my superior, he would issue orders to me assigning me tasks. One such order that I remember was when the supreme commander of the armed forces came to Knin. We had to search the ground along the side streets of the route that the supreme commander of the armed forces was to take. How many such tasks were issued to me by Colonel Budimir is something I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the picture that you've told us, it seems that you were reporting to both Colonel Budimir and Major Juric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be embarking on a new topic and that is probably a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd have a break first. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzolic. Mr. Dzolic, I want to ask you some questions now about daily tasks. You remember that phrase was asked of you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by that, we mean the daily tasks of the company of the military police. Is it right that daily tasks are matters such as guarding facilities, check-points, patrols?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They are routine matters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the investigation of crimes is not part of the daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Up to a point, you're right. What do I mean by this, Your Honour? For a company, and for me, the general military police in other words, these would be daily tasks. As for the crime -- the military crime police, these should be daily tasks, the investigation of crimes, if they had sufficient parameters to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the military police -- crime police, were a separate section of the 72nd and 73rd Battalions to your joint company. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The crime police was a different section of the 72nd Military Police Battalion; it was outside your company, your joint company.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: The crime police section of the 72nd Military Police Battalion did not -- was not part of the joint company in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And your daily task would not have included the investigation of crimes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: My tasks - and I'm speaking for myself - were not. So it was not part of my daily tasks to investigate crimes. As I said yesterday during my testimony, I think mention was made of this, from the 8th of August onwards, certain police, military police officers, were attached of the -- so certain military police officers of the crime police were attached to the Knin company. They were from the 72nd Battalion. And as of that moment on, they existed as an independent section of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just look at a document here, 65 ter 1677, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what we're going look at, Mr. Dzolic, is a book called "The Daily Order, Knin Joint Company, 5th of August to 23rd of September, 1995." And it's the daily order book for the Knin joint company, right from the start, when you were in Knin. Do you see that on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I see it, but I can't quite figure out the date here. I cannot see the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It says from the 5th of August to the 23rd of September, 1995, so it's right from the start, when you went to Knin.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you gave evidence yesterday, you looked at something called the duty log, which was a different book to this book. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just look at the first page in English. Your Honour, the translators of the Tribunal haven't reproduced all the names in the English translation for obvious reasons. The names of the individuals are in the Croatian version. This is how the Defence received the document off the Prosecution's 65 ter list, I should also add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this -- this book now? It's the daily order book, and it sets out the check-points. Do you see that? You've got names on yours. I'm going to have to -- yeah. There's a check-point of a company seen, check-point, and a list of names. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I just come back to what you said about the list of names. Now, this appears not to be just list of names because there's something added to it; for example, I could not expect someone to be by the name of motorist, for example, which there's apparently seems to be added something here there. For example, I'm looking at 14, 15, 16, and 17 of the list of 17 names. So, therefore, I would like perhaps if the Prosecution could assist here as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I could deal with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not of importance to me. I appreciate it may be to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties agree that it is not of any importance, then I will not insist. I just observe that there is more than just list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm corrected in the accuracy, Your Honour, of my explanation. I'm being brief. It is unimportant for the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if Ms. Mahindaratne would agree with that, then -- Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It apparently is what Mr. Kay tells us is that this is the unrevised translation uploaded on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is correct. And we are in the process of trying to upload the revised translation. It is just that I did not have notice that this document would be called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the time being, it appears to be not a major problem that we do not have this translated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to the second page of the B/C/S, keeping on the English page, so that I can marry it up. More names. Can we go to the page after that is correct, please. There you are. Ah, just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see down at the bottom there, "Bosko Dzolic," your name, Mr. Dzolic, as number one, left-hand corner? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we could turn the next page of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see daily order of the joint company for the 9th of August there; check-point towards Drnis; check-points -- it lists check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then the next page of the B/C/S, please; next page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It refers to securing the hotel, car patrol, auto patroller, and motorists, and details there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page again of the English -- actually, sorry, scroll down the English. It's my mistake. I'm very sorry about that. If we could go back on the English page. Sorry, Mr. Monkhouse. Down at the bottom, daily order, and then if we could move over the B/C/S page. And taking it on to the right-hand side, daily order, 6th of August, 1995, check-point towards Drnis; lists of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this book, Mr. Dzolic, as being the daily order book for the joint company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it right that if we went through further of these pages of this book, we would see details each day of the check-points, security of a building, and patrols set out, as to what individuals were doing them each day and what their shift hours were?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes. That is evident from this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've no need to go further into this book, as we will take up a great deal of time in just confirming what I have said and what you have confirmed to me. And is it right to say that this reflects the daily tasks of the joint Knin company, being the daily tasks of check-points, securing buildings, and patrols?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D787.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D787 is admitted into evidence. I take it that a revised translation will be sooner or later be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The parties will liaise on that, and I hope the Court appreciates that I haven't taken you through all these pages in what would be an exercise the Court could do for itself on the premise of the questions and the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Dzolic, that you went to several briefings at Mr. Cermak's office in Knin whilst you were there during the period the 5th to 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: It's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that at those meetings, there were a number of civilian people, people interested in the water, electricity, the functioning of the town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was not just a military meeting, but it was a meeting of many different people, all of whom were interested in the functioning of the town at that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at that meeting, various people would state what was happening in the matters that were important to them; for instance, a man interested in the electricity being put on in the town would be talking about that. Is that right? Is that an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That cleaning up the streets of the town; removing rubbish and debris was discussed.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot state that with certainty, but I think it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right, there were ten to 20 people gathered at these briefing sessions?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that Mr. Cermak chaired that meeting and was trying to coordinate between the different people and interests to help them --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were there as a representative of the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you the only military policeman present at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that with certainty; but, generally speaking, I think I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you recollect if there was a man from the civil police there, representing the civil police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think, as far as I can recall, that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the government's commissioner, Mr. Pasic, Mr. Petar Pasic, also present?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I do not recall that name, but I assume that he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that these briefings lasted for under one hour each morning?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot recall for certainty, but I think we can confirm that they did not take very long. They did not last very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But during the meetings whilst you were there, was it right that check-points were discussed as to the best places around the town for check-points to be put in place?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I cannot recall that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember if crimes that were happening, such as looting or burning, were discussed at the briefings that you went to?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember that that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect Mr. Cermak telling you at those briefings it was important for the military police to do their job?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I think that General Cermak did stress such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that General Cermak, at those meetings, was trying to get, as best as he could, the town of Knin working?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think that that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that General Cermak was not in a position, he could not order you to investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cermak had no authority to order you to investigate crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What Cermak -- what General Cermak could do was, in fact, ask you to attend meetings with him and the other people within Knin so that you could take part in the meeting. He couldn't order you to attend those meetings. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just quote, and perhaps in fairness if the witness is asked to take off his earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second, Mr. Dzolic. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has testified at paragraph 37. If could I draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to paragraph 37 of his first statement P875, that is the 2004 statement. He clearly testifies that -- he says: "I was also under the command of General Cermak, and I was to obey any order that General Cermak gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this statement the witness has gone through in proofing, and he did not correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now the witness is testifying differently to that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least that is a possibility that that can happen, when you're testing evidence, it sometimes comes out; and, of course, finally, the Chamber will have to decide what weight to give to part of his evidence which is contradictable, whether to draw any conclusion from that. But, Ms. Mahindaratne, cross-examination would not make much sense if we would have to accept that anything that is in evidence in chief should not be touched upon. I mean, cross-examination is there for testing and for challenging the evidence that was given in chief, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I agree with that. But my question is considering the demeanour of this witness and, clearly, his partiality to one party. I thinks, perhaps, that it is appropriate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, first of all, it is your witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, but sometimes the part -- the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is all comment. You're raising a lot of questions that may cross our minds at any moment in the future, how, what may be more credible parts of evidence, less credible part, more reliable, less reliable. But that should not, at this moment, interrupt the evidence Mr. Kay is eliciting from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is true, Mr. President. I just rose to my feet just to address Court and perhaps ask guidance from Court whether this would be an appropriate time to warn the witness under Rule 91, considering the -- the move from the original evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, I think I'll consult with my colleagues whether we will follow or not follow your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not follow your suggestion, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Kay, you may please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you got -- oh, you have got your headphones on, Mr. Dzolic. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've now forgot my question, if the Court would just forgive me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was about orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There we are, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that you were just invited to go to those briefings with the other people at General Cermak's office in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was no question of him ordering you to go to those meetings; you viewed this as just being an invitation.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I would like now just to look at a couple of documents that have been in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we look at P513, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dzolic, I'm showing you an order signed by General Cermak on the 8th of August concerning the UNCRO UN peacekeeping force, and about their movement on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we scroll it up a little bit higher, please. I mean the other way, sorry, down. Yes, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see this is signed by General Cermak, dated the 8th of August. It is sent to UNCRO elements, sent to UNCRO. And you were aware, were you not, that United Nations were in a compound within Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just make a correction, it is not sent to UNCRO elements. It is sent to the addressees which are mentioned at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm dealing with this. I'm trying to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see on the document that it says down here "Knin military police." Can you see that, Mr. Dzolic, bottom left-hand corner? Can you see it? Can you see "Knin military police," bottom left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever receive this order?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember having received it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document at all?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If a document was properly addressed to you as the commander of the joint company for Knin of the 72nd, is there a way that it should be particularly written in the address?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: In the address?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the correct way of directing a document to you, putting just those words "Vojnoj Policiji Knin"?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at the next document, 65 ter 2732.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is dated the 8th of August, 1995. It concerns the Croatian army and UNCRO soldiers, it's an order controlling the entrance to the UNCRO barracks, it's about checks on refugees, it's from General Cermak. First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't recall this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see at the bottom left-hand corner of the document it just says: "To military police."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that be a correct way to address a document, so that it reached you as the commander of the joint company in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: It would be more correct if it had said Knin military police; however, I allow for the possibility that this kind of letter, with this kind of title or name listed in the addresses, could have arrived in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next document, P512. That previous document, may we admit it into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D788.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D788 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we turn to P512, with my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document here, again from General Cermak, is an order about inspecting UNCRO helicopters and various other matters. It says: "To military police." Firstly, did you -- do you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty that I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document, D303.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, this is a document dated the 9th of August, 1995, and it concerns some UNCRO vehicles that were stolen from the UNCRO base. And an order was issued by General Cermak, asking for a team of people to be made up from members of the military police and from the MUP, with the task of finding UNCRO vehicles that are listed: A Nissan pick-up, Nissan Pajero, Toyota Land Cruiser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, to the extent you are summarizing the document, the word "asking" should be "ordering" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ah, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because that is what the document says. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ordering, I will correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't say that I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever become involved in searching for UNCRO vehicles, being the two Nissans and a Toyota Land Cruiser in Knin, as part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember, but one of our tasks was to search for stolen vehicles, if we had either information or an order concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had that as a task obviously; but did you, in particular, in relation to these UNCRO vehicles, did you set up a team from your military police and go out looking for the UNCRO vehicles identified here? Is that something that you did?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't assert with any certainty that I did that. I don't remember. But if such an order arrived, then probably the criminal police were instructed to investigate this, and the patrols were instructed that should they find such vehicles at -- or if they should see them at the barrier check-points, that these vehicles should be confiscated and brought to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And one more document we'll look at on this same issue, D503.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of August. Again, it concerns UNCRO property, engineering equipment, and vehicles that were stolen. And an order by Mr. Cermak was issued, asking for teams to be formed from the MUP, Knin military police, to find a bulldozer, road-leveller, mine sweeper, earth digger, a truck, six other vehicles, and a Land Rover. First of all, do you recognise this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you again summarized the document and you made the same mistake as you did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I used the word order, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard and I see transcribed "asking" for teams to be formed, and that's what I heard, as a matter of fact. If I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I used the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if I made a mistake, then I did it together with the transcriber, and I do not see anyone else jumping up and saying no, so I clearly heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Orie. If you look at line 22, page 44, Mr. Kay said: "And an order by Mr. Cermak was issued, asking for teams ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see. Yes, "an order asking for," and I commented on "asking for." It seems even to be -- but I reacted on a word "asking for," because earlier I did the same for "asking for." I do agree with Mr. Cayley that you now combined "an order" and included "asking for."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is nothing hanging on this. I'm not playing any games over these two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying that you're playing games, of course; but there is an issue about whether orders could be given or whether people were invited or asked for certain matters. That appears to be an issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Sorry. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: The document as such is not familiar to me. I don't remember having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you form any teams looking for UNCRO equipment, such as this?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall having formed a team, and this date as I see is the 12th of August and I had left Knin at that time. I don't know when this order arrived in Knin. I don't believe it arrived on the morning of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Although we have looked at some written orders here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Obviously, something is wrong with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this problem still exist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, yes. We will wait for the technician. It now says "technical difficult," but it apparently has been resolved. Mr. Kay, I may have misunderstood the word "asking" earlier as being equivalent to "seeking" rather than to "request." That becomes clear to me now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
