utterances.text: We'll resume now, Mr. Dzolic, okay? Right. Although Mr. Cermak may have issued orders such as these concerning --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may address Court, I think Mr. Kay's question and last answer of the witness has not been recorded due to the technical difficulty, where the witness said that he left on 12th August and he is not certain if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That appears not on the transcript. Perhaps you could invite the witness to repeat everything he said after he said that the document, as such, was not familiar to him. Could you please repeat what you said after you said "I don't remember having seen it," and you added another part. Could you please repeat that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date on the document is the 12th of August, 1995. That's the day when I left Knin. I don't know when this order arrived in the Knin company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Although General Cermak issued these orders, do you agree that, in fact, he was not in a position to command you to take these actions; it was for you to decide whether you undertook any obligation he may have referred to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. That is seeking an opinion from the witness. The facts are before Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. I'll re-read the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Directly concerns the witness, Your Honour, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are several elements in the question. The first one is seeking the judgement of the witness on whether, in the position of Mr. Cermak, he could command the witness; and second is whether he was free not to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- undertake any obligation he referred ... If you could just try to split it up in small portions, then we'll find out what the knowledge of the witness is and to what extent you're seeking opinion or judgement or assessment of a certain situation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, isn't it the case that you did not have to follow any obligation referred to you by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As far as I can remember and recall the work and the coordination of work, while I was the company commander in Knin, it's my opinion that I was not obliged to follow orders of this kind as orders; however, as information that something had occurred, that is, that certain vehicles had been stolen, I was supposed to take steps in accordance with my possibilities to have these vehicles found. In these cases, a search warrant should have been issued rather than an order. Why this is entitled "order" is something I can't say. I can't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that you would not have to report back to Mr. Cermak on any such matter that we have been looking at?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't say that with any certainty. As an order, this was not something I had to report about; but if I had found these vehicles, it would have been in order to inform whoever had asked for these vehicles to be searched for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look now at another document dated -- sorry. 2D06-0001. This is a document dated the 17th of August, 1995, from the 72nd Battalion Military Police. It is signed by Major -- Commander Major Mihael Budimir and is sent to the companies of the military police. And in this order, it sets out a rotation of military and police forces. And in paragraph 2, it states: "First Lieutenant Luka Orsulic is selected as the Knin military police joint company commander, "and names other officers after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, can you confirm that that is Lieutenant Orsulic who took over the command of the joint company after you had left on the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it refers to the rotation in Knin and various details. Are you able to help us with paragraph 3 as to what that means, concerning the rotation in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, as I understand this order, for the rotation in Knin, the commander of the 1st company of the general military police shall select 29 officers; the 2nd company commander," that was me, "shall select 40 members; and the traffic company commander shall select 18 members. The rotation in Knin refers to the forces that were in Knin while I was commander; and when I left, they remained under the command of Captain Luka Orsulic. And they were sent back to their original units on leave and in their place, members of those companies that are listed in point 3 of this order arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see in paragraph 4: "The crime investigation military police department chief ..." Are you able to tell us who that person was, the name of that individual?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Boro Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. "The duty service leader and logistic platoon commander shall select the rotation for their offices." Can you explain that paragraph, please, if you are able to?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Are you referring to paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of this order makes the crime investigation military police department chief, the duty service leader, and the logistic platoon leader responsible for selecting their officers. The officers who are on the ground would be brought back, and they would be replaced by other officers who would be designated in that work sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This would not be a function, then, of the commander of the joint company in Knin, Lieutenant Orsulic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I am not following you. What do you mean? Which function was not the function of Lieutenant Orsulic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The crime investigation department of the military police organised itself and its rotation of staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this same pattern, and when I attempted yesterday, you know, Mr. Kay would insist on foundation. Now I would insist, Mr. President, that -- what is the foundation. The witness -- is the witness aware of these rotations or is he just merely commenting on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is invited to comment on the document, and the question Mr. Kay puts to the witness suggests that he has knowledge of what happened. And I agree with you that it would certainly better assist the Chamber if we would know about the source of knowledge which goes beyond what we find in the document. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did identify through the witness, hoping that that matter was dealt with, who the particular chief was, which obviously the witness knew, and then sought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this question goes further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware, from your position and work in the 72nd Battalion of the military police, of the operations -- of the methods of operating of the crime investigation department of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I was not aware of the methods of their operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't detain any more time on this, Your Honour; it's controversial. Can we go to document 65 ter 2984. May the last document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D789 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 2984 is a document dated 22nd of August, and it's from the military police administration, sent to the 66th Battalion of the military police. It concerns the safety of the Knin command post commander, General Cermak. It's an order. It concerns an analysis in relation to the purpose of security of him. It's an order that the commander of the 72nd Military Police will conduct all the necessary steps for General Cermak's security whilst moving or still from the -- from the forces of the 7th Company, and it gives various steps. We see in paragraph 3 that it refers to Lieutenant Orsulic again, and that's the order signed by a commander Colonel Damir Kozic, which is on page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, do you know who Colonel Kozic is?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Colonel Damir Kozic was, I believe, the chief of the general military police section in the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page of the English, because reading the signature again and again is not very exciting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This concerns security of General Cermak being ordered to be provided by the 7th Company of the Knin military police. You told us, is it right, that it was the joint company while you were there but it later became the Knin 7th Company? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And to order such measures for the security of General Cermak, is that a usual route, is that the proper way for the military police to deal with the matter through the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As I understand it, it is the proper way to carry out assignments of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D790 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One other document to look at, 2D06-0013. This is a document dated the 21st of August from the commander of the military police in Knin, Lieutenant Orsulic, who sent this matter to the military police administration. It's a report on carrying out security. It concerns security on the 19th of August, 1995, when the military police in Knin secured a Ministry of Defence working group touring military facilities with two military policemen, and informs what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This report from Lieutenant Orsulic goes to the military police administration. Is that a correct way to report on such a matter, within the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I cannot state that with any certainty. What do I mean? This type of report, in my view, was to be sent to the 72nd Company [as interpreted] of the military police. That would have been the regular procedure. Then from there, it would be forwarded to the administration. However, it is possible that based on an order by the military police administration, which would have had to contain their use, employment in this type of assignment, it is possible that such an order had an item where it stated that the commander of the -- of the 7th Company, in this case, Lieutenant Orsulic, could directly address the addressee, within the police administration -- military police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have look at the left bottom part of the English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, could just address Court, at page 8 [sic], line 15, there's a reference to "72nd Company," and that could be a translation error. I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 8 of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At line 15, I just wanted to bring to Your Honours' attention so that maybe you could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honour is finished with this document, I have no further questions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just looking at it, but I had to then switch to LiveNote to look at it. No, I was just -- could it be moved up again now a little bit. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And maybe just to, as I think about it, help on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you said, the usual way of reporting would have been from the Knin company up to the commander of the 72nd Battalion, who was Major Budimir at that time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. On another matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D791.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D791 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On another matter, I want to ask you a question now about your -- your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we have P875, please, produced, and go to paragraph 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want you to look carefully at paragraph 37 of this statement, please, Mr. Dzolic, and if you could just read it to yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in these words, which say: "The way I understood it was that I was still under the command of Colonel Budimir, but that I was also under the command of General Cermak, and I was to obey any order that General Cermak gave me." And it's that passage there that I want to ask you questions about. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are those your words, Mr. Dzolic? Did you say that: "The way I understood it was that I was still under the command of Colonel Budimir, but that I was also under the command of General Cermak, and I was to obey any order that General Cermak gave me." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't think that's the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that statement wrong?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: For a part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it wrong to say that you were under the command of General Cermak and to obey any order that General Cermak gave you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may address Court, I think perhaps this is an appropriate time to again renew my application under Rule 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I would like to make submissions on the matter, if it is appropriate for me to do so, in case of anything the Court might do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's still a reason to make submissions on the matter, if you would know that the Chamber will not follow the suggestion by Ms. Mahindaratne, then you are free to do so; but the Chamber will not follow the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I ask the question again, Mr. Dzolic? We've had an interruption, and you may have forgotten it. Is it wrong, as written here, that "... I was also under the command of General Cermak, and I was to obey any order that General Cermak gave me."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As I understand this statement, it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, is it wrong to say you were under the command of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I was not under the command of General Cermak; I was under the command of Colonel Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it wrong to say that you were to obey any order that General Cermak gave you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic, you'll be next in line. Mr. Dzolic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dzolic. I am counsel for General Markac, and I will put a few questions to you. And I realize that a lot of time has elapsed since 1995, but I would appreciate if, to the best of your recollection, can you go back to those events. Mr. Dzolic, do you know General Markac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I wasn't looking at the clock when you started your cross-examination. Rather than to interrupt after five or six minutes, perhaps it is better that we take the break first and that you then, in one breath, can do your cross-examination rather than to be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate your suggestions, Your Honour. That would be suitable for Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzolic, good afternoon one more time. My question, before we took the break, was the following: Do you know General Markac?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Not in person. I just know of him from the media and from the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his function was at the time of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please pull up document 65 ter 318.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, in a moment, we will see the rules on the structure and work of the military police of the armed forces of the Croatia. Have you had opportunity to see this -- these rules earlier?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These rules are dated February 1994. Can you confirm that this -- these same rules were in force in the second half of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I believe that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 2 of these rules, Article 4, ERN 707; page 2 of the body of the text. This is just the contents page; so, in fact, if we could see page 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will now go through these rules, Mr. Dzolic. It is stated here that members of the military police, and I'm referring to Article 4, were active military personnel, part of whom were organised in military police anti-terrorist units and who had the status of professionals. Speaking of anti-terrorist units, are you familiar with these units and do you know what their tasks were in 1995 in August and onwards?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or perhaps we can approach this from another angle. Article 4 of this -- of these rules speaks of anti-terrorist units. You can see that, right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 11 of the rules -- could we please pull up Article 11, and that's two pages on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 11 of these rules states that anti-terrorist units of the military police are to carry out tasks as contained in Article 9, as it says here, and that that is their primary purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I would like it point out to the Judges that there is obviously an error here, because Article 9 only has one item, so reference should be made here to Article 10, which has several subparagraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the primary purpose of the anti-terrorist units of the military police is, according to those rules - and now I'm quoting Articles 8 and 9 of -- or paragraphs 8 and 9 of Article 10 - is to carry out -- to participate in combat with sabotage and other enemy units, and in providing -- and providing security --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are these rules in keeping with your understanding of what it is that the military police are to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the last portion of the Article. Could you please repeat that, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. I'm just checking transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote: "The role and purpose of anti-terrorist units under these rules," specifically in Article 8 -- or, rather, item 8 of Article 10, where it is stated that "those units participate in the fight against sabotage, terrorist, rebel, and other enemy groups." Is that in keeping with how you understand the role of anti-terrorist units of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, please tell me this: Were there any members of anti-terrorist units in your company while you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember that there were such members in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to Article 5 of these rules describing the uniform of the members of the military police. In peace and war, members of military police in the service wear the official HV uniform, a white belt, a while pistol holster, a pistol, a white baton, restraining devices, and a military police shield on a regulation base attached to the upper pocket on the left side of their upper garment. Can you see that portion, Mr. Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what colour was this official uniform and what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: At what point in time? Which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the months of August, September, and October, in 1995; in other words, during and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't remember exactly. I do not have the image in front of my eyes what the uniform that was worn at that time was like. I assume, because there were combat activities on, that we were in camouflage uniforms. However, there was a period of time when military police units had, let's call them, drab-colour uniforms, solid colour. Now, what exact time -- at what exact time this uniform was worn, I cannot really say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, did anti-terrorist units have the same uniforms as the general military police or did they wear some other type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I think that members of the anti-terrorist units also had drab -- olive-drab uniforms. I'm not sure, and I cannot claim this with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the belt was like, what colour was it, and also what was the colour of the pistol holster? I'm referring to the members of the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: They wore green military belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It seems obvious from your answer that the belt was not white, as in the -- as with the uniforms of the general military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's right. However, there were times when anti-terrorist units, if that was necessary, during security assignments they could also wear, as required, white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what caps members of the anti-terrorist units wore, what kind of caps?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty, but I think they were black berets, like those worn by all members of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on these black berets there were two badges on the front?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what badges these were?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: There was the coat of arms, the badge of the military police; and the coat of armies, which was the badge of the anti-terrorist units of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Article 7 of these rules refers to motor vehicles of the military police, and motor vehicles of the military police shall be painted green, while the door and the cover -- or, rather, the engine hoods and the back will be painted white; the trunk lid are paint the white; and that motor vehicles are marked at the front doors; and the engine hoods with the a triangular sign, that there is a stylized falcon with the words "military police." This corresponds to your description, Mr. Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 10 of the same rules refers to the tasks and assignments carried out by the military police and the scope of activities, and it contains a description of the jobs and tasks; that is, the protection of life and security of all persons, prevention and uncovering of crimes, identification and arrest of perpetrators of crimes. These are, in fact, tasks from the purview of crime military police?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: What tasks do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Uncovering crimes, discovering and arresting perpetrators of crimes within the jurisdiction of military judicial bodies, these were the tasks of the crime police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Is that paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Item 3 refers to the safety of road traffic, military road traffic; and this was done by the traffic unit of the military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the members of that unit, compared to other units of the military police, have special insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Are you referring to the military police traffic police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Sometimes, I think, when checking road traffic, they had white sleeve covers. I'm not sure whether they always wore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they also - that is, the members of the traffic military police - have those stop signs they would use to stop traffic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, and it said military police on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Article 12, towards the bottom of the page, it says, in chapter IV, which refers to the powers of the members of the military police, and it goes on in Article 15, to speak in detail of those powers. So let's look at Article 15, and we will see that, according the rules, the military police has the following powers, and then there are several pages detailing the powers of the military police. These are warning; and then under 2, identification; item 3, submitting a report, and that's on the next page; then 4, bringing in. It says here that members of the military police bring in military personnel and civilians when they are perpetrators of a crime that falls within the jurisdiction of a military court. Does this correspond to your recollection and the practice that prevailed while you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Bringing persons in could be done pursuant it a court order, or to an arrest warrant, or if the person was caught in the act while violating military discipline or committing a crime; and all this was the job of the military police, among other jobs. Then item 5 deals with detention. Mr. Dzolic, in your company, did you have any premises in Knin where you could detain persons who had been caught committing a crime or for whom an arrest warrant had been issued until you could hand them over to the appropriate court?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember that we had any special premises used to detain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What, then, was the procedure? If a person needed to be deprived of their liberty for these reasons, either because they had been caught in the act committing a crime or a breach of discipline or if an arrest warrant had been issued for that person, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If, in practice, the need arose for a person to be deprived of their liberty, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: You mean in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: While I was the commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: We would temporarily detain that person in a room that was available, and as soon as the conditions were in place to escort that person to military detention facilities which existed in Split. We didn't have them. The person would be escorted to the military detention facility in Split. Also, if the need arose for that person to be brought before an investigate military judge, the person would be taken with an escort to the appropriate Military Court. However, I wish to mention that during the time I was the commander there, I don't remember any such cases occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that reply. Then is the further powers of the military police, according to the rules we have on our screen. We've been through detention. On the next page, item 6, we have use of physical force; use of batons; restraining. So these were the powers that the military police had at their disposal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. Dzolic, in certain situations as a military policeman, and the members of your company were able to use other means of coercion and even weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: If the need arose in line with our power, yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were also able to use dogs for protection and for searches. Did you have this possibility?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: While I was in Knin, we didn't have such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Dzolic, we come to item 12, which speaks of the powers of the military police to search homes, other premises, and persons. And it says here that members of the military crime police or other authorise the personnel of the military police could search apartments, premises, and persons; and it says here in what cases this could be done and whether a search warrant was needed from a court, whether it was one a person was caught in the act of committing a crime or asking for assistance, and so on. Mr. Dzolic, my question is the following: During the time you were in Knin, was this power of the military police used? Did your military policemen, when needed, search homes and other premises in the area where you were responsible?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: If the need arose, yes, this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: One more question in question to these rules, Mr. Dzolic. I'm referring to Article 62, which says that a citizen of the Republic of Croatia, who is not a member of the Croatian army, in other words a civilian, and who has been deprived of his liberty because he has been caught in the act committing a crime, falling within the jurisdiction of an another regular court, is to be taken immediately by the authorised military policeman to another -- to a local body of the Ministry of Interior with a report on the crime committed and the grounds for arrest. So this is the situation where -- this is a situation where a military policeman has to intervene in relation to a civilian and such things did happen, did they not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember any such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, in accordance with the rules, the military police were authorised to intervene in relation to civilians, in certain situations; for example, when the civilian was caught committing a crime, either on his own or together with military person, a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is included in the 92 ter submission, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, Mr. Mikulicic, it should be a P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be on the list which we have not yet finally received, I think; but then there is no need to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's all the same for me, whether it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is in evidence; that's the important thing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, I asked you at the outset whether you knew General Markac. If I remind you that General Markac was the commander of the special police of the Ministry of Interior, does that jog your memory? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Well, yes, as I already said, I know about it from the media and from television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you said that the military police cooperated with and coordinated certain actions with the civilian police of the Ministry of Interior. I am thinking especially of barrier check-points, patrols, and similar situations. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, was there any such cooperation with the members of the special police of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't remember that in Knin itself. I don't remember that there was such cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, judging by external characteristics, would you be able to recognise a member of the special police of the Ministry of Interior if you were to run into such a person?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I would, if he had all the insignia on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, may I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. When asked whether there was such cooperation between the military police and the members of the special police of the Ministry of Interior, you said: "I don't remember that in Knin itself." Do you have any recollection as to whether such cooperation existed outside of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but I do allow for the possibility that there was such cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to this question: Are you referring to cooperation in combat activities during the combat that was part of Operation Storm, or after the end of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When asked by His Honour, you now you said you an allowed for the possibility that somewhere outside Knin itself there might have been cooperation between members of the military police of the Ministry of Defence and the special police of the Ministry of Interior. My question is the following: When you said that, were you thinking of cooperation in the course of combat activities as part of Operation Storm, or were you referring to cooperation after the end of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such cooperation in the course of Operation Storm, which does not exclude the possibility; but I was primarily thinking of before and after Operation Storm, in carrying out tasks of providing security for the supreme commander and similar tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. Mr. Dzolic, I would now like to refer to paragraph 13, Exhibit 517, where you said that you had occasion to familiarize yourself through training with the rules of war. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that each member of the police, in the course of this training, was issued a booklet with a short version of the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: If I recall -- the way I recall it, it should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... booklet already in the evidence under D533.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzolic, military police members had to undergo special training when compared to other members of the Croatian army. That is indisputable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Do you mean did I have to be trained or dressed in different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean trained. They had to undergo a different type of training as compared to other members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Well, part of their training would have to be specialised training which other soldiers would not have to undergo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any especially trained de-mining expert in your company?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I don't recall that there were any such members in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your 2004 statement, paragraph 22 and 35, you said that when you arrived in Knin, you set up check-points at the outskirts or on the approaches to the town. Can you remember, was it immediately after your arrival that the check-points were manned by both members of the military police and the regular police, or not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, when we first arrived there, we did not have joint barrier check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by "later on." I can't really be sure; but as far as I can remember, we manned the barrier check-points together later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: One of the purposes of these check-points was to search individuals and vehicles that went or drove through the check-point. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there instances where you resorted to the powers as derived from the rules that we saw a minute ago? I'm referring to detention of individuals that were in a motor vehicle -- or, rather, the confiscation of items found in the vehicles, which pointed to the possibility of team that having been confiscated in the course of a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically, but it is possible that there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was a special warehouse that was set up to house these items?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: While I was the company commander, I don't remember that we had any particular warehouse or depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see P879.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, I will now show you a document that has been introduced by the Prosecution of -- dated the 5th of August, 1995, that was submitted by Major Juric, and it referred to August 5. You've already seen this document, but I would like now to discuss item -- or paragraph 6 of this document, where it is stated that the military police has searched the terrain and the villages of Vrlika and Knin, some portions of them. Could you tell us what kind of operation was this, the search of the terrain, and who in the military police would carry out such an operation of searches of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I can't remember this because this was not even in my area, Vrlika and Knin. I can't remember this. It says here that the terrain was searched, in part, and reference is made to Vrlika and Knin. I don't recall who was involved in this. It wasn't my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see document, since we mentioned Major Juric, D2868 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: D268, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to correct myself. If we're talking about the search of the terrain and the city itself, it is possible that we were involved in this; but I don't understand what the author of this report, Major Juric, meant, when he said the searches of terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the second page of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, this is an order that you have already seen today. It was shown -- it was issued by the chief of the military police administration, Lausic, where certain tasks and authorities are conferred on Major Juric. It is stated here that Major Juric is to be the commander of the 72nd and 73rd Battalion of the military police, that he is responsible for the implementation of all police tasks, that he shall cooperate and coordinate the implementation of tasks with the workers of, and then it lists the Zadar-Knin police administration, the Sibenik and Split Dalmatia, then the assistant for SIS, the security and information service of Split, the chief of the SIS, and the Croatian army commanders in the Split area of responsibility and Sjever area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, since Mr. Mikulicic is reading back, what we have in the English translation is that -- If we could go back, Mr. Registrar, to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was reading from page 1 of the original text.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is says is that he is superior to 72nd military police and 73rd military police commanders with regard to 73rd, and so on. Now Mr. Mikulicic read it as it is stated here that Major Juric is to be the commander of the 72nd and 73rd battalion, so perhaps the exact language being read back might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, there seems to be an issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I said so there, it is my mistake obviously. It is written that he is not commander. Okay. I think that is my mistake. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were reading the tasks that were assigned to Major Juric --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was my primarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... whether commander or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzolic, we can see here that no mention is made of members or units of the special police of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia. From your recollection, was Soldier Ivan Juric ever a superior to the units of the special police of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would now like to explore your statement, and I mean paragraph 32 of your 1994 -- 2004 statement, where you said that on the 6th of August, 1995, there were 140 to 150 military policemen in Knin and that there were some difficulties in their work. And in your statement of 2008, you said, in Article 8, that there was not a sufficient number of military policemen and that there should have been at least twice as military policemen. Could you tell us what led you to the conclusion that the number of military policemen was insufficient to carry out the tasks in Knin while you were there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: In addition to an insufficient number of men to provide security that was required in order to carry them out, because the area was slowly expanding and we needed a far greater number of officers, in order to cover the entire area, as it was being done in Knin town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, as time went by, units -- or, rather, military police stations were also formed in other towns. You're aware of that, right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 1614 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is another order of -- issued by Mate Lausic, dated 5 August 1995, where he orders that units of the military police be established; and as you can see in the penultimate paragraph, mention is made of a platoon of military police in Gracac and one platoon of military police in Donji Lapac. Were you aware of this process of setting up new units in the newly liberated towns an areas?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: I was not aware of it, at least not as far as these areas mentioned here are concerned, except that I know that the joint company came to Knin and established a company there, and I assumed that it is possible that it was as it's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have been advised by my case manager that this document, as well, is on the bar table list from the Prosecution that has been submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a look at that list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It is included in the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a look at the list of annexes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the very same situation, Your Honour, as regards to two other documents that I was intend to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this is the document -- well, the one is -- no, my mistake. Sorry. These are documents already tendered as evidence. One is D399, which is about the establishment of the platoon of military police in Gracac on 7th of August, 1995; and the other one is D293, from 8th of August, that has been finished the establishment of the platoon, military police, in Gracac, and in Donji Lapac is finished with an establishment of the military police station in Donji Lapac. So I'm just referring to those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is D293, and did you say D399?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are drawing your attention to the relevance of those documents in relation to the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... established in those two cities. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. I would like, however, that you finish in two or three minutes, so that we have three or four minutes left to deal with some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me check my subjects. Yes. I would like just one more topic, which shouldn't be too long. May I? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzolic, I have one more question and then we will finish up for today, and I mean the creation of the duty service of the military police. You have already explained what their function was. What I would like to know is: What was the level of cooperation between the duty service of the military police with the -- with the counterpart, the duty service of the civilian police of the Ministry of Interior. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO DZOLIC [Resumed}
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't recall what the level of cooperation was. Please don't misunderstand me. There probably was some cooperation, the operative duty services, but I don't know what the parameters were of that cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. You will be further cross-examined by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My understanding is Mr. Mikulicic will continue in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will continue in the morning for about half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will continue in the morning, and you said how much? You said half an hour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me. Mr. Dzolic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning in another courtroom, Courtroom I, at 9.00, so that your cross-examination can be continued; and perhaps you will be further re-examined and perhaps questions by the Bench will be put to you. I again instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, whoever it is, about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the programme for testimony. Mr. Mikulicic, you said you would need half an hour. And then, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I had asked for two hours. I am going to be under that, Your Honour. I am going to try, try, to stay at about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About an hour. That would mean that there is a possibility that we could finish the cross-examination within the first session. Ms. Mahindaratne, then re-examination, how much time you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, based on the material, of course, this is without the Gotovina case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to guess on what time. Of course, as matters stand now, there is always --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As matters stand now, Mr. President, it would be about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About 20 minutes. Which means that if the Chamber would have some questions as well, that we might finish in the second session tomorrow morning. Now, we know that there is another witness waiting, the witness who will be called next, and who is scheduled, from what I understand, for examination-in-chief of one hour, is it? Ms. Mahindaratne, will it be you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that would be Mr. Hedaraly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... aware of that, yes. So that would be one hour. I have got no idea on how much time the Defence would need for cross-examination because we are considering whether there's a possibility at all to have a bit more time than perhaps tomorrow in the afternoon, so that we can finish the cross-examination, but that heavily depends on the estimates of the time needed for the next witness. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I probably have two, two and a half hours perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two, two and half hours. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Presently, Your Honour, we don't have any cross-examination for this witness, but we might reconsider our position tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is the same position with Markac Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean that with an extended session tomorrow, that there is an fair chance that we would be able to hear the testimony of the next witness. Is there any problem as far as Defence teams are concerned to continue tomorrow in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no problem, Your Honour, but this is an matter I have to raise with you in relation to my attendance tomorrow. But perhaps I could deal with that after you have conclude this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would not be an obstacle for -- okay. Then Mr. Registrar was exploring the possibilities. We have no final answer yet. What will be possible or will not be possible is still to be seen, but the parties should prepare for a continued session tomorrow in the afternoon. I take it that it would be mainly the Gotovina cross-examination that would take substantial time tomorrow. Yes. Thank you for this information. You will be kept updated by either Chamber staff or by Mr. Registrar about what to expect. Mr. Kay, there was a matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, I'm not able to be here tomorrow for very good reasons of a longstanding nature that have to be dealt with and can only be dealt with tomorrow, and a matter that has been scheduled for sometime. Mr. Cayley will be in charge of the ship in my absence and dealing with matters arising. There is no disrespect intended to the Court or the witness, but it was anticipated originally that the witness would be shorter in direct examination when I spoke to Mr. Hedaraly and Mr. Waespi earlier in the week. It didn't turn out that way, but it's one of those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one of the advantages of counsel and co-counsel, that the one can take care if the other is not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I don't think at this moment there are any -- oh, yes, there is one tiny little matter. Today someone said that he -- when something was done not exactly as it should have been done, someone said that Mr. Monkhouse -- that he sent his apologies to Mr. Monkhouse; whereas, our usher usually deals with cutting out the relevant portions on our screen. And I just would not let it happen that the role of the usher is ignored, so I put this as a correction on the record. If there's nothing else, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter. I don't know but I am advised by e-mail about MFI P887. I don't know if the Prosecution intended to tender that exhibit or not; but if so --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that is a reference to -- I believe Mr. Misetic is referring to document 2406?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that was not included in the 92 ter submission and that was merely in the exhibit list, and I did not tender it in the course of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it can be stricken as number 8 from the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I want it get rid of this list now as soon as possible; that is, on this list, we see 65 ter numbers 318, 1614, 1999, 456, 5445, 1433, 5467. Numbers were assigned by Mr. Registrar P880 up to and including P886; and since there are no objections, they're all admitted into evidence. Now, Mr. Registrar, number 8 is off this list, which means that 1598 remains. Would that keep the same number or would it have to be renumbered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1598 now is assigned number P887, that's different from what we saw on our list, and is also admitted into evidence. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
